questions.question: What are constraints in SQL and why are they important?
questions.title: SQL Constraints — Enforcing Data Integrity
questions.direct_answer: **Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**. The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**. They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the main constraint types and that they enforce integrity at the DB level.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Stress that constraints are the last line of defense — enforced even if app code is buggy.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Constraints** enforce data integrity at the database level.
- **Core types**: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT.
- **Enforced on every write**, by every client.
- **Last line of defense** even if app validation fails.
- **FOREIGN KEY** prevents orphan rows across tables.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Constraints are rules you attach to your tables that the database enforces automatically, rejecting any insert or update that breaks them. Their whole purpose is data integrity: they keep the data valid no matter which application, script, or person is writing to the table. The main constraints are primary key, which uniquely identifies each row and is both unique and not null; foreign key, which links a column to another table's primary key and enforces referential integrity so you don't get orphan rows; unique, which prevents duplicate values; not null, which forces a column to always have a value; check, which enforces a custom condition like salary greater than zero; and default, which supplies a fallback value when none is given. The reason I always define constraints at the database level, rather than relying only on application validation, is that they're the last line of defense. Application code can have bugs, and often more than one service writes to the same database, so a constraint guarantees that even if the app logic fails, genuinely invalid data simply can't get in. The only caution is not to over-constrain, where an overly strict check ends up blocking legitimate edge cases.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

sections.title: Constraints at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|PRIMARY KEY|~row identity|unique + not null|one per table|often auto-increment
emerald|FOREIGN KEY|~links tables|references a PK|enforces referential integrity|CASCADE options
amber|UNIQUE / NOT NULL|~value rules|UNIQUE = no duplicates|NOT NULL = must have value|
rose|CHECK / DEFAULT|~custom + fallback|CHECK = condition|DEFAULT = fallback value|enforced on write

sections.title: Constraints in a CREATE TABLE
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id        INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,      -- unique identity
  email     VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,         -- required + no duplicates
  dept_id   INT REFERENCES departments(id),       -- foreign key
  salary    DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),     -- custom rule
  status    VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'          -- fallback value
);

-- this fails the CHECK constraint:
INSERT INTO employees (email, salary) VALUES ('a@x.com', -100); -- rejected
```

*The database rejects the negative salary regardless of what the app sent.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping DB constraints**: trusting app validation alone — a second service or a bug can insert bad data.
- **No NOT NULL on required columns**: lets NULLs slip into mandatory fields.
- **Missing FOREIGN KEY**: orphan rows (a child pointing to a deleted parent).
- **Over-constraining**: overly strict CHECKs that block legitimate edge cases.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

questions.question: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint in SQL?
questions.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know PK is unique+not-null+one-per-table while UNIQUE allows NULL and can repeat.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking UNIQUE forbids NULLs, or that you can have multiple primary keys.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note PK auto-creates a clustered index in many DBs and is the natural FK target.

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
sections.content:
Both enforce **no duplicate values**, but they differ in three ways. A **PRIMARY KEY** is the row's identity: it's **UNIQUE and NOT NULL**, and there's exactly **one** per table. A **UNIQUE** constraint also blocks duplicates but **permits NULL** values, and a table can have **many** unique constraints.

PRIMARY KEY is what other tables reference via foreign keys, and in many databases it backs the **clustered index**. Use PRIMARY KEY for the identifier (`id`); use UNIQUE for additional columns that must not repeat, like `email`.

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
sections.content:
blue|PRIMARY KEY|~row identity|unique + NOT NULL|one per table|FK target, clustered index
emerald|UNIQUE|~no duplicates|allows NULL|many per table|e.g. email, username
amber|Shared|~both reject duplicates|both can be composite|both back an index|
rose|Choose|~by role|identifier -> PRIMARY KEY|other no-dup column -> UNIQUE|

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
sections.content:
| Aspect | PRIMARY KEY | UNIQUE |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicates | not allowed | not allowed |
| NULLs | not allowed | allowed |
| Per table | exactly one | many |
| Role | row identity | extra no-dup rule |
| FK target | yes (typical) | possible |

sections.title: Misusing UNIQUE as the identity
sections.content:
```sql
-- email can be NULL, so it's a poor row identity
CREATE TABLE users (
  email VARCHAR(120) UNIQUE,   -- allows NULL, can't reliably identify a row
  name  VARCHAR(80)
);
```

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for email
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,  -- unique + not null identity
  email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- no duplicates, and required
  name  VARCHAR(80)
);
```

*`id` identifies the row; `email` is unique but is not the identity.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use a **PRIMARY KEY** for the column (or columns) that identify a row — typically a surrogate `id`. It's the natural target for foreign keys.

Use a **UNIQUE** constraint for any *other* column that must not contain duplicates but isn't the identity — email, username, phone, SKU. Add `NOT NULL` alongside UNIQUE when the value is also required.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PRIMARY KEY** = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, one per table.
- **UNIQUE** allows NULLs and can appear many times per table.
- **Both** prevent duplicate values and back an index.
- **PRIMARY KEY** is the usual foreign-key target.
- **Use PK** for identity, **UNIQUE** for other no-duplicate columns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Primary key and unique both stop duplicate values, but they play different roles. A primary key is the row's identity. It's unique and also not null, and a table has exactly one primary key. Because it reliably identifies each row, the primary key is what other tables point to with foreign keys, and in many databases it also backs the clustered index that physically orders the data. A unique constraint also prevents duplicate values, but it has two key differences: it allows null values, usually one or more depending on the database, and you can have many unique constraints on a single table. So the way I choose is by role. The column that identifies a row, typically a surrogate id, gets the primary key. Any other column that must not repeat but isn't the identity, like email, username, or a product SKU, gets a unique constraint. And if that unique column is also required, I add not null alongside it, which effectively gives it primary-key-like strictness without making it the actual identity. The classic mistake is using a nullable unique column like email as the identity, which is fragile because nulls and changing emails make it a poor identifier.

questions.question: What is a FOREIGN KEY constraint and what does CASCADE mean?
questions.title: FOREIGN KEY Constraint and CASCADE in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **FOREIGN KEY** is a column that references the **PRIMARY KEY** of another table, enforcing **referential integrity** — you can't insert a child row pointing to a non-existent parent. **CASCADE** propagates parent changes to children: `ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes child rows when the parent is deleted; `ON UPDATE CASCADE` updates the key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand FK referential integrity and ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming you can delete a parent row that still has children, or misusing CASCADE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare CASCADE vs SET NULL vs RESTRICT and warn that CASCADE can delete more than expected.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **FOREIGN KEY** references another table's PRIMARY KEY.
- **Enforces referential integrity** — no orphan child rows.
- **`ON DELETE CASCADE`** deletes children with the parent.
- **`SET NULL`** nulls the reference; **`RESTRICT`** blocks the delete.
- **Use CASCADE carefully** — it can delete more than expected.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A foreign key is a column in one table, the child, that references the primary key of another table, the parent. Its job is to enforce referential integrity, which means the database guarantees the relationship is always valid. So you can't insert an order that points to a customer id that doesn't exist, and by default you can't delete a customer who still has orders, because that would leave orphan rows pointing at nothing. CASCADE and the other referential actions control what happens to the child rows when the parent changes. ON DELETE CASCADE means deleting a parent automatically deletes all its children, so deleting a customer also deletes their orders. ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the child but sets its foreign key to null, which requires the column to be nullable. ON DELETE RESTRICT, which is effectively the default, blocks the delete entirely as long as children exist. There's also ON UPDATE CASCADE, which propagates a change to the parent's key down to the children. The one warning I always give is to use CASCADE deliberately, because a single delete at the top can cascade down and remove a huge amount of data if your tables are deeply related. So I match the action to the business meaning of the relationship.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

sections.title: FOREIGN KEY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~links child to parent|references parent PK|referential integrity|no orphan rows
emerald|ON DELETE CASCADE|~delete children too|parent gone -> children gone|tidy, but powerful|can delete a lot
amber|SET NULL|~keep child, null link|parent gone -> FK = NULL|column must be nullable|
rose|RESTRICT / NO ACTION|~block the delete|parent kept if children exist|safe default|

sections.title: Foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting to delete a parent with children**: blocked unless you set CASCADE/SET NULL.
- **CASCADE deleting too much**: `ON DELETE CASCADE` can wipe large subtrees — use deliberately.
- **SET NULL on a NOT NULL column**: invalid — the FK column must be nullable.
- **Type mismatch**: the FK column must match the referenced PK's type.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks the delete while children still exist. This is the safe default.
ON UPDATE CASCADE copies a changed parent key down to the children.

beats.text: Picture orders linked to customers with ON DELETE CASCADE. You delete customer five. The database removes that customer and all their orders in one shot. Here's the non-obvious part. One delete at the top can wipe a whole tree of related rows below it.

Reaching for CASCADE everywhere, then losing more rows than you meant to.
SET NULL on a NOT NULL column, which simply can't work.
A foreign key type that doesn't match the parent key type.

questions.question: What is the CHECK constraint in SQL?
questions.title: CHECK Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **CHECK** constraint enforces a custom **boolean condition** on column values — the database rejects any insert/update where the condition is false. Examples: `CHECK (salary > 0)`, `CHECK (age >= 18)`, `CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE'))`. It pushes validation into the database itself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know CHECK enforces a custom condition at the DB level.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on app validation, or assuming older MySQL enforces CHECK (it ignored it pre-8.0.16).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note CHECK treats UNKNOWN (NULL) as passing, and mention enum-style CHECK with IN.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CHECK** enforces a custom boolean condition per row.
- **Rejects** any insert/update where the condition is false.
- **NULL passes** a CHECK (use NOT NULL to require a value).
- **Great for** ranges, positivity, and enum-style `IN` lists.
- **Old MySQL (<8.0.16)** ignored CHECK — check your version.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A CHECK constraint lets you enforce a custom boolean condition on a column directly in the database. Every time a row is inserted or updated, the database evaluates the condition, and if it's false, the write is rejected. This is how you push business rules into the schema itself instead of relying purely on application code. Common examples are CHECK price greater than zero to forbid negative prices, CHECK age greater than or equal to eighteen, CHECK rating between one and five for a range, or CHECK status IN a list of allowed values, which gives you an enum-like behaviour. A subtlety worth mentioning is how CHECK treats nulls. A CHECK passes when the condition is true or unknown, and a comparison with NULL is unknown, so a null value generally satisfies the check. If you actually need a value, you combine the CHECK with a NOT NULL constraint. Another important caveat is historical: MySQL before version eight point zero point sixteen would parse a CHECK constraint but silently ignore it, so on older MySQL you couldn't rely on it; modern versions enforce it properly. And one limitation: CHECK is per-row, so it can only reference values in the same row, not other rows or other tables; for cross-row rules you'd use triggers or application logic.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

sections.title: CHECK at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~custom condition|boolean expression|rejects false rows|business rules in schema
emerald|Examples|~common rules|salary > 0|age >= 18|status IN (...)
amber|NULL behaviour|~unknown passes|NULL satisfies CHECK|add NOT NULL to require|
rose|Gotcha|~MySQL history|ignored before 8.0.16|enforced now|verify your version

sections.title: CHECK constraints in action
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  price  DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (price > 0),
  rating INT CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  status VARCHAR(10) CHECK (status IN ('NEW','USED'))
);

INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 50.00, 4, 'NEW');   -- ok
INSERT INTO products VALUES (2, -5.00, 4, 'NEW');   -- rejected: price > 0 fails
INSERT INTO products VALUES (3, 20.00, 9, 'NEW');   -- rejected: rating out of range
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **App-only validation**: skipping CHECK lets a buggy or second client insert invalid values.
- **Forgetting NULL passes**: a NULL value satisfies CHECK — add `NOT NULL` if a value is required.
- **Assuming old MySQL enforces it**: before 8.0.16 it was ignored.
- **Cross-row logic in CHECK**: CHECK is per-row; it can't reference other rows/tables.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

questions.question: What is the DEFAULT constraint in SQL?
questions.title: DEFAULT Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **DEFAULT** constraint supplies a value for a column when an `INSERT` doesn't provide one. It keeps columns populated with sensible fallbacks — `status DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'`, `created_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`. Note: explicitly inserting `NULL` overrides the default; omitting the column triggers it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know DEFAULT applies only when the column is omitted, not when NULL is given.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting DEFAULT to replace an explicitly inserted NULL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention function defaults like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and pairing DEFAULT with NOT NULL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DEFAULT** supplies a value when the column is omitted on INSERT.
- **Explicit NULL overrides** the default (NULL is stored).
- **Pair with NOT NULL** to force the fallback to apply.
- **Supports functions** like `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`.
- **Use for** sensible starting states, not validation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A DEFAULT constraint gives a column a fallback value that the database uses when an insert doesn't provide one for that column. It's how you keep rows sensibly populated without making every insert spell out every column. Typical examples are status defaulting to active for a new user, created_at defaulting to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP so each row records when it was created, or a counter defaulting to zero. The rule that catches people is the difference between omitting a column and explicitly inserting null. The default only applies when you leave the column out of the insert. If you explicitly insert NULL, the database stores NULL and does not substitute the default, because you actively asked for null. So if you want the fallback to always win and never allow a null, you combine DEFAULT with a NOT NULL constraint; then an attempt to insert null is rejected and the default is what you get when the column is omitted. Two more tips: defaults can be functions, not just literals, which is how CURRENT_TIMESTAMP works for timestamps, and I treat defaults as convenient starting states, not as validation, because real validation belongs in CHECK constraints, not in defaults.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

sections.title: DEFAULT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~fallback value|used when column omitted|keeps rows populated|sensible starting state
emerald|Examples|~common defaults|status = 'ACTIVE'|created_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP|count = 0
amber|Rule|~omit vs NULL|omit column -> default used|explicit NULL -> NULL stored|defaults don't override NULL
rose|Pair with|~NOT NULL|DEFAULT + NOT NULL|fallback always applies|blocks explicit NULL

sections.title: Explicit NULL skips the default
Omit the column (or add NOT NULL) to use the default
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT,
  status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',  -- NOT NULL forces the fallback
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO users (id) VALUES (1);
-- status = 'ACTIVE', created_at = now() -> defaults applied
```

Sample row:

| id | status | created_at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ACTIVE | 2026-06-04 10:00:00 |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting DEFAULT to replace explicit NULL**: it only applies when the column is omitted.
- **No NOT NULL with DEFAULT**: callers can still store NULL explicitly.
- **Static value where a function is needed**: use `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, not a hard-coded date.
- **Relying on DEFAULT for required business data**: defaults are fallbacks, not validation.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

speakable_v2.standard_example: A users table with status DEFAULT active and created_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
speakable_v2.hook: A DEFAULT fills in for a missing column. But insert null on purpose and it steps aside. It'll keep your null instead.

beats.text: A DEFAULT constraint gives a column a fallback value. The database uses it when an insert leaves that column out. So your rows stay filled in, and you don't repeat every column each time.
Lots of columns have an obvious starting state. A new user is active. A row's created time is right now. A counter starts at zero. A DEFAULT sets that for you, so the insert stays short and clean.

items: Use a literal like a status of active or pending.
Use a function like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP for a created time.
Pair DEFAULT with NOT NULL to force the fallback to win.
Treat a DEFAULT as a starting value, not as real validation.

beats.text: Say status has a DEFAULT of active. Skip the column on insert and the row comes out active. Here's the non-obvious part. Insert null on purpose and the database stores null, not active. The default only fires when you leave the column out entirely.

items: Expecting a DEFAULT to replace an explicit null. It won't.
Skipping NOT NULL, so a caller can still store a null.
Hard-coding a date instead of using CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
Leaning on a DEFAULT for required business data.

speakable_v2.cap: So a DEFAULT covers the missing column. An explicit null still wins, so pair it with NOT NULL when it matters.
followup_handoff: If you INSERT NULL explicitly into a DEFAULT column, what value is stored?
What is DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP used for?

questions.question: What is the NOT NULL constraint in SQL and how is it different from an empty string?
questions.title: NOT NULL Constraint vs Empty String in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **NOT NULL** forces a column to always contain a value — an insert/update that leaves it NULL is rejected. An **empty string** (`''`) is a *known* value of zero length, which is completely different from **NULL** (unknown/missing). A NOT NULL column still happily accepts `''`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish NULL (missing) from an empty string (a real, zero-length value).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming NOT NULL also blocks empty strings.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add a CHECK (length > 0) when you must forbid empty strings, since NOT NULL alone won't.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **NOT NULL** requires a value; rejects NULL on write.
- **Empty string `''`** is a known, zero-length value — not NULL.
- **A NOT NULL column** still accepts `''`.
- **To forbid blanks**, add `CHECK (LENGTH(TRIM(col)) > 0)`.
- **Test NULL** with `IS NULL`, not `= ''`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: NOT NULL is a constraint that forces a column to always contain a value, so any insert or update that leaves it null is rejected. But the key thing to understand is that null and an empty string are completely different. Null means the value is unknown or missing; an empty string is a real, known value that simply has zero length. Because the empty string is a genuine value, a NOT NULL column will happily accept it. So if I declare a name column as NOT NULL, inserting null is rejected, but inserting an empty string succeeds, because that empty string counts as having a value. That surprises people who assume NOT NULL also blocks blanks. If my actual rule is that the column must contain real text, NOT NULL on its own isn't enough; I add a CHECK constraint like CHECK length of trimmed name greater than zero, which rejects both null and empty or whitespace-only strings. The trim matters, because a string of just spaces would otherwise pass a naive length check. This null-versus-empty distinction also shows up in queries: WHERE column equals empty string will not find null rows, so you have to use IS NULL for those, and in a JPA entity a nullable column should map to a wrapper type rather than a primitive.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

**NOT NULL** forces a column to always contain a value — an insert/update that leaves it NULL is rejected. An **empty string** (`''`) is a *known* value of zero length, which is completely different from **NULL** (unknown/missing). A NOT NULL column still happily accepts `''`.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

sections.title: NOT NULL vs Empty String
sections.content:
blue|NOT NULL|~must have a value|rejects NULL|enforced on write|required field
emerald|Empty string ''|~known, zero-length|a real value|passes NOT NULL|different from NULL
rose|NULL|~unknown/missing|fails NOT NULL|IS NULL to test|not the same as ''
amber|Forbid empty|~need more|NOT NULL + CHECK(LENGTH>0)|blocks both NULL and ''|

sections.title: NOT NULL alone lets empty strings in
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);

INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (NULL);  -- rejected (NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('');    -- ACCEPTED: '' is a real value
```

sections.title: Add a CHECK to forbid empty strings too
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL CHECK (LENGTH(TRIM(name)) > 0)
);

INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('');     -- rejected by the CHECK
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ravi'); -- ok
```

*`NOT NULL` blocks missing values; the `CHECK` blocks blank ones.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking NOT NULL blocks `''`**: it doesn't — an empty string is a valid value.
- **Treating NULL like `''` in queries**: `WHERE col = ''` won't find NULLs; use `IS NULL`.
- **Mapping nullable columns to primitives in JPA**: use wrapper types for nullable columns.
- **Forgetting TRIM**: a string of spaces passes a naive `LENGTH > 0` check.

sections.title: How the choices differ
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the NOT NULL constraint in SQL and how is it different from an empty string? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: A name column declared NOT NULL on a users table
speakable_v2.hook: NOT NULL stops missing values, not blank ones. An empty string sails right through, because to SQL it counts as a real value.

beats.text: NOT NULL means a column must always hold a value. An empty string's a real value with zero length. So they're not the same thing at all. Null means missing or unknown. An empty string's known and fully present.

Use NOT NULL when a column must always carry some value. That'll block the missing case. But if you also need to forbid blanks, NOT NULL won't do it alone. Add a CHECK on the trimmed length so empty and space-only text gets rejected too.
Declare name as NOT NULL. Insert null and the database rejects it. Insert empty quotes and it'll go straight in. That's the gotcha. To block both, add a CHECK on the trimmed length.

speakable_v2.cap: So NOT NULL blocks the missing value, while an empty string is a real one. Use a CHECK to ban both.
